claims.text: The target regime consists of noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing at least five elements.
The balance between configurational entropy and limited atomic diffusion governs final crystal-structure selection under rapid thermal transitions.
High configurational entropy favors single-phase formation.
Limited atomic diffusion promotes partial elemental segregation.
Slower heating and cooling provide more time for elemental intermixing.
Slower heating and cooling suppress segregation and stabilize a single-phase solid solution.
The initial material is a near-equimolar mixture of at least five noble-metal precursors.
Heating and cooling rates will be varied from approximately 100 K/s to approximately 1 K/s while precursor composition is held constant.
Elemental ratios, atmosphere, and peak temperatures will be controlled while ramp rates are varied.
Transient high-temperature atom mobility determines the extent of interdiffusion relative to entropic mixing.
Enhanced diffusion at slower ramp rates allows configurational entropy to produce more thorough mixing into a single phase.
Rapid heating and cooling restrict diffusion and thereby cause partial segregation and multiphase regions.
Relative to a fast-ramp baseline, slower ramps will produce fewer secondary phases, more uniform elemental distributions, and a larger single-phase fraction.
A ramp rate of approximately 100 K/s produces limited diffusion time and frequent segregation or secondary phases.
The hypothesis applies to compositions containing at least five noble metals processed under inert or reducing conditions.
The process must reach a peak temperature high enough to initiate precursor decomposition.
Local precursor interactions and support effects may complicate rate-driven outcomes.
Obtaining identical single-phase structures with no significant phase or segregation dependence across 1–100 K/s would falsify the hypothesis.
